# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

A noisy alarm trains people to ignore it, and a missing runbook turns every incident into a search. On AWS the good practice is a burn-rate alarm pair (a long window and a short window) joined by a composite alarm, a runbook that starts with the CloudWatch evidence, and an escalation message that carries numbers, a log line and a verdict about the infrastructure.

In this lab you deploy a small shop stack on EC2 with an EBS data volume. A checkout incident repeats every 30 minutes (:20–:24 and :50–:54 UTC) because the data filesystem fills up. You tune two burn-rate alarms offline, build them and a composite alarm in the console, then analyse the incident as an EC2 and EBS log analysis: application log, system log, disk metric, EBS volume metrics and instance health. You finish with the runbook and the escalation evidence.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: You hand the right team a complete evidence package, not a vague complaint. |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: You rule out EBS and EC2 with metrics before you blame the application. |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Your alarm pages for real outages only and links to a runbook that works at 3 a.m. |

The EBS volume vol-… (2 GiB, /dev/sdf) is the data disk. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

The EC2 and EBS log analysis follows the path of the problem from the user to the disk. Each step answers one question and narrows the cause.

*Figure: EC2 / EBS Triage Path — App Log (what fails) → System Log (kernel message) → Disk Metric (how full) → EBS Volume Metrics (is the service healthy) → Instance Status (is the host healthy)*

| Step | Where in the Console | Question | Healthy Looks Like |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| App log | Logs Insights, /shop/\<seat\>/lab4/app | What error do users get? | No ERROR lines |
| System log | Logs Insights, /shop/\<seat\>/lab4/system | What does the kernel say? | No XFS / I/O messages |
| Disk metric | Metrics, ShopLab4/\<seat\>, DataDiskUsedPercent | How full is the filesystem? | Below 80 % |
| EBS volume | EC2 → Volumes → Monitoring (AWS/EBS) | Is the EBS service slow or erroring? | Low queue length, normal write ops, idle time high |
| Instance | EC2 → Instances → Status checks and Monitoring | Is the host healthy? | 2/2 checks passed, CPU low |

## 1.4  Learning Objectives

• Design a long and a short burn-rate alarm and test the design offline against three scenarios

• Create CloudWatch alarms on a metric-math expression and a composite alarm in the console

• Query an application log and a system log with CloudWatch Logs Insights

• Read EBS volume metrics (VolumeWriteOps, VolumeQueueLength, VolumeIdleTime) and the instance status checks

• Conclude whether EBS, EC2 or the filesystem is the cause

• Write a runbook and an escalation message with evidence

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Burn-Rate Alarms and the Composite Alarm

A **long** alarm (is it serious?) and a **short** alarm (is it still happening?) each compare the burn rate with a threshold. The composite alarm rule ALARM("u07-burn-long") AND ALARM("u07-burn-short") pages only when both are true: sustained and current. The alarm threshold in percent is the burn rate times the budget (14.4 × 0.5 % \= 7.2 %). CloudWatch alarm periods are 1, 5, 10, 15, 30 or 60 minutes.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| One problem should produce one page. The child alarms have no notification; only the composite alarm notifies, and only when the outage is real and still running. |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: EBS Problem vs Full Filesystem

An error that mentions a device or XFS can look like a storage problem. EBS metrics tell you whether the **service** is slow (queue length high, operations failing). A full filesystem produces "No space left on device" while the EBS volume itself is idle and healthy. The owner differs: platform or application team for capacity, AWS support for a real EBS fault.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With Storage Incidents |
| :---- |
| Blaming EBS because the volume is named in the kernel line. Check VolumeQueueLength and VolumeWriteOps first; if they are normal, the disk service is fine. |

## 3.3  Logs Insights and Metrics You Need

| Item | Query or Metric | Use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| App errors | filter level \= "ERROR" \| stats count(\*) by message | Top error |
| System log | filter @message like /No space left/ \| sort @timestamp desc | Kernel message |
| Disk | ShopLab4/\<seat\> → DataDiskUsedPercent (Maximum) | How full |
| EBS | AWS/EBS → VolumeWriteOps, VolumeQueueLength, VolumeIdleTime | Volume health |
| Instance | EC2 status checks, CPUUtilization | Host health |

| **2.A Which settings did you choose and how many minutes after the outage start does the page come?**  Answer:  `long_period_min = 15`, `short_period_min = 1`, `burn_threshold = 14.4` (7.2 % error rate), and `for_min = 0`. In Scenario B, the outage starts at minute 20 and the page arrives at minute 22 — **2 minutes** after the outage starts.  |
| **2.B Why does the composite alarm need both a long and a short alarm?**  Answer:  The **long window (15 min)** filters out brief, transient spikes (such as Scenario A's 2-minute spike) so they do not exhaust enough error budget over 15 minutes to trigger a false page, while the **short window (1 min)** ensures rapid recovery/reset as soon as an outage is mitigated rather than keeping the page stuck in alarm for the remainder of the 15-minute window.  |
| **2.C Write the composite alarm rule.**  Answer: ALARM("u07-burn-long") AND ALARM("u07-burn-short")  |
| **2.D The old rule (error ratio above 1 % for 1 minute) — what did it do on scenarios A and C?**  Answer:  It produced **false-positive pages** on both: **Scenario A (brief 2-minute spike):** Paged immediately at minute 20 despite the spike resolving quickly without threatening the monthly SLO. **Scenario C (slow 1.2 % leak over 6 hours):** Paged immediately at minute 0 on a low-burn leak that does not require urgent on-call intervention.  |

|  |

| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Step 1: "Order write failed: No space left on device (/data/orders)" × 392 (five incident minutes) |
| Step 2: "kernel: XFS (nvme1n1): metadata I/O error: No space left on device (data volume at 90-100%)" in the minutes :20-:24 |
| Step 3: DataDiskUsedPercent ≈ 60-63 normally; 90, 95, 98, 99, 100 in :20-:24 |

| **3.A Record the top application error, the system log line, the disk peak and the EBS verdict.**  Answer: Top error: Order write failed: No space left on device (/data/orders). System log: kernel: XFS (nvme1n1): metadata I/O error: No space left on device. Disk peak 100 %. EBS verdict: normal (no abnormal queue length or write operations). |
| **3.B The kernel line names nvme1n1. Why is this still not an EBS fault?**  Answer: The device name only says where the filesystem lives. The error text is "No space left on device" (full filesystem) and the EBS metrics show an idle, healthy volume; a real EBS problem would show high queue length, errors or stalled operations. |
| **3.C Which team owns the fix and what is the first mitigation?**  Answer: The platform / infrastructure team (filesystem capacity on the instance). First mitigation: free space (delete old files, rotate logs) or enlarge the EBS volume (modify the volume size, then grow the partition and filesystem). |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Composite alarm rule rejected | Child alarm names wrong or not created yet | Alarm names | Create the two child alarms first; names are case-sensitive |
| Period not accepted | Unsupported alarm period | Alarm settings | Use 1, 5, 10, 15, 30 or 60 minutes |
| No EBS metrics | Looking at the root volume or too early | Volume ID | Use the 2 GiB /dev/sdf volume; wait a few minutes |
| Logs Insights empty | Wrong group or range | Log group name | Select /shop/\<seat\>/lab4/app or /system and a range including :20-:24 |
| Access denied | Wrong region or name without seat id | Top-right region | Allowed region only; names start with the seat id |
| Spike pages in the replay | Long period too short or threshold too low | replay output | Raise long period or threshold |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — Ruling Out EBS |
| :---- |
| Which two EBS metrics ruled out a volume problem? |
| What would you have seen in a real EBS fault? |
| Key insight: Rule out the infrastructure with metrics before escalating to the application team or AWS. |

| Discussion 2 — One Page per Incident |
| :---- |
| What would on-call receive without the composite alarm? |
| How do two windows reduce false pages? |
| Key insight: Long \= sustained, short \= still happening; both must be true. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Blaming EBS from the device name | The volume is in the message | Wrong team paged | Check VolumeQueueLength and write ops |
| Alarm on one datapoint | Default setting | False pages | Two alarms and a composite |
| Alarms with notifications on each | Easy setup | Several pages | Notify only from the composite |
| Runbook without commands | Written from memory | Useless at 3 a.m. | Include the queries and the first mitigation |

| Extension A — Slow Leak Ticket |
| :---- |
| Design a third alarm for scenario C (burn about 2.4 for hours) that creates a ticket and not a page. |
| Key question: which period and threshold? |

| Extension B — Disk Alarm |
| :---- |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — CLOUDWATCH EC2 / EBS COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Alarm | Static \> 7.2 on ErrorPct (100 \* m1 / m2) | Burn 14.4 × 0.5 % |
| Composite | ALARM("\<seat\>-burn-long") AND ALARM("\<seat\>-burn-short") | One page |
| App log | filter level \= "ERROR" \| stats count(\*) by message | Top error |
| System log | filter @message like /No space left/ | Kernel line |
| EBS | VolumeWriteOps · VolumeQueueLength · VolumeIdleTime | Volume health |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

**INSTRUCTOR ONLY — remove this appendix from the learner copy if you do not want learners to see the set-up details.**

1\. One sandbox AWS account (never production) and ONE allowed region; learners need a default VPC in that region.

2\. IAM users u01–u40 (user name \= seat id) with INSTRUCTOR-learner-iam-policy.json from lab2-slo-cloudwatch (replace REGION and ACCOUNT\_ID). It denies other regions.

3\. Template check once before class: deploy as one seat; within 5 minutes ShopLab4/\<seat\> metrics and both log groups must show the :20-:24 and :50-:54 incidents (history for 3 hours is written at start-up).

4\. SIMULATED parts: the application metrics, the app log and system log lines and DataDiskUsedPercent are generated by shop\_sim.py on the instance. REAL parts: EC2, EBS, the AWS/EBS metrics, status checks, CloudWatch alarms and Logs Insights. The EBS volume is genuinely idle — that is what learners must notice.

5\. UNVERIFIED: the template, user-data, agent timestamps, IAM policy, EBS metric availability for an idle gp3 volume and CloudShell availability were not tested in a live account.

6\. Cost: 40 × t3.micro \+ 2 GiB EBS for about two hours, custom metrics and log ingest: a few USD; clean-up: delete the stacks and the alarms.
